newsitem.title: GERMANY: German court to rule in Algerian gun-running trial.
newsitem.headline: German court to rule in Algerian gun-running trial.

text.p: A German court is due to pass a verdict on Monday on two sons of Algerian fundamentalist opposition leader Abassi Madani charged with smuggling arms and explosives from Europe to anti-government forces in Algeria.

Prosecutors have asked the Duesseldorf court to give two years and eight months jail to Salim Abassi and two years four months to his brother, Ikbal, for charges including explosives offences, belonging to a criminal group and document forgery.
They have also asked for sentences of two years and seven months and 11 months for two other Algerians, Nasr-Eddine Layachi Hemaz and Mahmoud Logbi facing the same charges in the 10-month trial.

The four men all deny involvement. They have been in custody for almost two years since authorities cracked down on Algerian fundamentalists using Germany as a base to support an armed conflict against Algeria's military rulers.
They are accused of belonging to a gun-running group that worked independently but kept links with other Islamic fundamentalist groups in France, Italy, Belgium and Algeria.

The group is alleged to have shipped around 100 assault rifles, over 30 machine pistols, 20 repeating rifles, 15 hand guns, eight pump guns and assorted ammunition and explosives to Morocco and Algeria between March 1993 and April 1994.
The weapons were allegedly sent to the Armed Islamic Group (GIA) and the Islamic Salvation Army (AIS), the military wing of the fundamentalist Islamic Salvation Front (FIS).
The Abassis' father, Abassi Madani, is co-founder of the FIS, which took up arms against Algeria's military rulers after they intervened in 1992 to scrap a general election the FIS was set to win.

Abassi Madani was sentenced to 12 years jail in 1991 in Algeria. He was put under house arrest in 1994. His sons Ikbal, Salim and Oussama fled to Germany in 1992 and were been allowed to stay as political refugees.
